facts.statement: The modern basic Hiragana syllabary contains 46 standard kana representing morae, including the five vowels あ, い, う, え, and お.
The あ-row is あ a, い i, う u, え e, and お o; these vowel sounds anchor the organization of the Japanese kana table.
The か-row is か ka, き ki, く ku, け ke, and こ ko.
The さ-row is さ sa, し shi, す su, せ se, and そ so; し is read shi rather than si in standard Hepburn romanization.
The た-row is た ta, ち chi, つ tsu, て te, and と to; ち and つ have irregular romanized forms.
The な-row is な na, に ni, ぬ nu, ね ne, and の no.
The は-row is は ha, ひ hi, ふ fu, へ he, and ほ ho; ふ is commonly romanized fu rather than hu.
The ま-row is ま ma, み mi, む mu, め me, and も mo.
The や-row has や ya, ゆ yu, and よ yo; modern standard Hiragana does not use standalone yi or ye kana.
The ら-row is ら ra, り ri, る ru, れ re, and ろ ro; the Japanese r sound is distinct from English r and l.
The わ-row is わ wa and を wo; を is primarily the object particle and is normally pronounced o in modern Japanese.
ん is the sole basic Hiragana kana for a moraic nasal and its pronunciation changes phonetically according to the following sound.
Dakuten marks transform parts of the か, さ, た, and は rows into voiced sounds: が, ざ, だ, and ば rows.
The dakuten rows are が ga, ぎ gi, ぐ gu, げ ge, ご go; ざ za, じ ji, ず zu, ぜ ze, ぞ zo; だ da, ぢ ji, づ zu, で de, ど do; and ば ba, び bi, ぶ bu, べ be, ぼ bo.
Handakuten marks transform the は-row into the p-row: ぱ pa, ぴ pi, ぷ pu, ぺ pe, and ぽ po.
ぢ and づ occur in specific vocabulary and spelling patterns, while じ and ず are more common; learners should verify each reading in a complete word.
Contracted yoon sounds combine a kana from the i-row with small ゃ, ゅ, or ょ, as in きゃ kya, きゅ kyu, and きょ kyo.
Common yoon families include しゃ sha, しゅ shu, しょ sho; ちゃ cha, ちゅ chu, ちょ cho; にゃ nya, にゅ nyu, にょ nyo; and ひゃ hya, ひゅ hyu, ひょ hyo.
Voiced and semi-voiced yoon families include ぎゃ gya, じゃ ja, びゃ bya, and ぴゃ pya, with corresponding small ゅ and ょ forms.
A small っ represents a geminate consonant and adds a mora, as in がっこう gakkou; it is not pronounced as an independent tsu syllable.
Long vowels must be learned from the word and context because their spelling varies by vowel sequence; do not infer pronunciation from isolated kana alone.
Hiragana is the primary kana script for native Japanese words, okurigana, grammatical particles, and inflectional endings; learn it alongside real vocabulary and sentences.
Kana recognition should be tested in both directions: identify the sound from the character and write or select the character from the sound.
Romanization is a temporary bridge; verified Japanese vocabulary and sentence context are the source of truth for pronunciation, particles, and sound changes.

relationships.description: The vowel and consonant rows organize the complete modern basic Hiragana table.
Dakuten and handakuten are systematic marks that extend the basic kana inventory.
Basic, voiced, and semi-voiced yoon combinations share the small ゃ, ゅ, and ょ spelling pattern.
Small っ and long-vowel spelling change timing and must be practiced in complete words.
Hiragana literacy develops through retrieval, vocabulary, sentence context, and reduced dependence on romanization.
